target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels because some countries already run on very high renewable electricity shares and because the U.S. history of alternative energy use is only a partial indicator.
objection: High renewable shares in a few countries do not show that alternative energies can scale to cover most of the energy demand of a large country; in the U.S., alternative energy use has never exceeded about 20%, which AG2 says demonstrates that alternatives have not historically reached the scale needed for broad fossil-fuel replacement.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as a fast, dependable low-carbon component of a fossil-free system.
objection: Nuclear power is too dangerous and ineffective as a serious global-warming solution, because accidents such as Fukushima can wipe out the carbon-free electricity gains, so nuclear cannot be counted on as a dependable rapid substitute for fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that electrification can cover many fossil-fuel uses and therefore electricity decarbonization can eliminate fossil fuels.
objection: Decarbonizing electricity and electrifying some end uses does not eliminate fossil-fuel use across the whole economy, because major fossil-fuel roles remain in transportation liquid fuels, industrial process heat, and chemical feedstocks that are not fully electrified.

target: AG1’s assumption that a renewables-plus-firm-low-carbon electricity system can satisfy all fossil-fuel end uses.
objection: Many non-electrified fossil-fuel services—especially process heat, chemical feedstocks, and parts of transport—cannot be fully and rapidly shifted to electricity-driven technologies alone at present, so AG1’s framework does not actually cover all fossil-fuel uses.

target: AG1’s claim that electricity can replace industrial fossil-fuel uses by being converted into heat and molecules.
objection: Converting electricity into industrial heat, hydrogen, synthetic fuels, and other molecules requires substantially more electricity per unit of useful output than direct energy use, so wholesale replacement would demand extremely large increases in electricity generation.

target: AG1’s argument that historical renewable deployment in high-performing countries shows scaling is feasible and that more electricity demand is not a fundamental barrier.
objection: Even if some countries have achieved high renewable shares, AG2 argues that the U.S. historical ceiling of about 20% alternative energy shows that alternative electricity has not reached the enormous scale needed for fossil-fuel replacement via electricity-to-heat-and-molecules pathways.

target: AG1’s view that the U.S. historical ~20% level does not prove alternatives cannot replace fossil fuels.
objection: Alternative energy has never exceeded about 20% historically in the U.S., and AG2 says this is evidence that alternatives have not approached the scale required for rapid, wholesale fossil-fuel replacement in a timeframe consistent with net-zero.

target: AG1’s claim that a fossil-free transition can happen quickly enough without a bridge fuel.
objection: Replacing fossil fuels requires replacing or retrofitting long-lived assets such as vehicle fleets, buildings, and industrial equipment, and that turnover is slow even when alternatives exist; therefore, near- and mid-term fossil elimination is constrained by capital stock turnover.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not needed as a bridge because firm low-carbon electricity can scale in time.
objection: Because rapid emissions reductions are needed while alternative systems scale, AG2 argues that natural gas is an appropriate and necessary bridge fuel, since existing infrastructure allows comparatively fast emissions reductions.

target: AG1’s claim that rapid power-sector decarbonization makes a bridge fuel unnecessary.
objection: Decarbonizing electricity does not automatically eliminate fossil-fuel carriers needed for non-electric end uses and fuel-dependent operations, so rapid clean power alone does not remove the near-term need for fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that firm low-carbon electricity makes natural gas unnecessary as a bridge.
objection: Even with firm low-carbon electricity, non-electric and fuel-dependent systems still need to be retrofitted or retooled, so fossil fuels can remain necessary in the near term; therefore, a natural-gas bridge remains justified.

target: AG1’s assumption that nuclear can provide the dependable firm power needed for near/mid-term replacement.
objection: Because nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective as a serious global-warming solution, it cannot be relied on as the dependable low-carbon backbone that AG1 needs for its near-term replacement pathway.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not a necessary bridge if electricity-based conversions are available.
objection: If nuclear cannot reliably provide the firm low-carbon power needed for electricity-based conversions, then those conversions cannot be assumed to deliver the dependable near-term emissions outcome AG1 needs, so fossil fuels—especially natural gas—remain necessary as a bridge.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables plus nuclear can cover reliability and backup functions without natural gas.
objection: AG2 argues that the reliability and backup roles attributed to natural gas can be met by firm low-carbon generation, but that such a system still does not automatically remove fossil dependence because some services are not instantly electrified and the replacement of those services is slow.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can replace fossil fuels in the near/mid term without a bridge fuel.
objection: Near/mid-term effective replacement requires rapidly scaling both low-carbon electricity and the conversion infrastructure for heat and molecules, and the U.S. historical record of only about 20% alternative energy use suggests that such scaling has not yet been achieved.

target: AG1’s claim that a clean electricity system is enough to eliminate fossil-carrier dependence.
objection: Effective replacement requires new alternative carrier supply chains—such as hydrogen, e-fuels, charging networks, storage, transport, and distribution—not just cleaner electricity generation, so alternatives cannot remove fossil-fuel necessity quickly enough.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as a rapid bridge in carrier replacement.
objection: Nuclear cannot be treated as a risk-free, dependable rapid bridge because accidents like Fukushima can wipe out carbon-free electricity gains, so fossil-fuel carriers would still be needed while new infrastructure scales.
